title: Moja soba
reviewerNotes: Full draft to Lesson 1 exemplar bar. ready for human review before publish.
storyBeat: Ana settles into the room above Amira’s and learns imati plus simple adjective agreement.

vocabulary: Name soba, kuća, stan, vrata, and prozor
Name krevet, sto, stolica, and lampa
Use velik, mala, lijepa, and udoban for size and comfort
grammar: Use imam and imaš for have
Match short adjectives to room words
Keep Moja soba as a ready possessive chunk
culture: Living above a café is a classic small-city arrangement
Visit Stolac and Radimlja as a stone-house postcard from Herzegovina

grammar.title: Imam / imaš
grammar.explanation: Imati means to have. Learn Imam for I have and imaš for you have. Say Imam sobu. Say Imam krevet. Ask Imaš lampu? Keep objects as chunks.

grammar.title: Moja soba
grammar.explanation: Soba is feminine, so moja soba is the natural chunk. Pair it with short descriptions. Say Moja soba je mala. Say Moja soba je lijepa.

grammar.title: Adjective agreement intro
grammar.explanation: Match the adjective shape to the noun you see. Feminine soba and kuća often take -a forms such as mala and lijepa. Masculine prozor and krevet take forms like velik and udoban. Learn the pairs by ear in this lesson.

culture.title: A room upstairs, and stone houses in Stolac
culture.body: Ana’s new address is a simple one, a small soba above Amira’s café. The window looks over the street, and the door never quite keeps Mrvica out. Emir widens the idea of home with postcards from Stolac in Herzegovina. Stone houses climb below the old town walls there, and the Radimlja stećci necropolis sits in open light nearby. Ana starts her home vocabulary in one rented room, and Emir’s postcards remind her that people across Herzegovina have lived in stone houses on this land for a very long time.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A: Name the room
lessonBlocks.body: Walk the space and name what you see. Learn soba, vrata, prozor, krevet, sto, stolica, and lampa. Add kuća and stan for the wider home map. Ana touches each object and says the word twice. Emir refuses English escape hatches. If you live above a café, you still need Bosnian for the furniture.
tips: Soba is a room. Stan is an apartment. Kuća is a house.
Point and name before you make long sentences

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B: Imam and short descriptions
lessonBlocks.body: Build short ownership sentences. Say Imam sobu. Say Imam krevet. Say Moja soba je mala. Say Prozor je velik. Say Krevet je udoban. Ana hangs a tiny Livno cheese postcard next to a Stolac photo, then discovers Mrvica already claimed the pillow. Ownership is a spectrum.
tips: Keep Imam, Moja soba je, and short adjective endings ready
Match mala and lijepa to feminine soba and kuća

conversation.title: Iznad kafića
conversation.setting: Ana’s room above Amira’s. Soft street noise, one suitcase, one judgmental cat.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.bosnian: Hvala! Moja soba je mala, ali lijepa.
lines.english: Thank you! My room is small, but beautiful.

lines.speaker: Emir
lines.english: Do you have a bed? A table? A chair?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.bosnian: Imam krevet. Imam sto. Imam stolicu.
lines.english: I have a bed. I have a table. I have a chair.

lines.speaker: Amira
lines.bosnian: Prozor je velik. Dobro za zrak.
lines.english: The window is big. Good for air.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.bosnian: Krevet je udoban. Volim moju sobu!
lines.english: The bed is comfortable. I love my room!

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.bosnian: Mrvica sjedi na jastuku. To je sada njen sto.
lines.english: Mrvica sits on the pillow. That is her table now.

lines.speaker: Emir
lines.bosnian: Ona ima sobu. Ti imaš sobu. Super!
lines.english: She has a room. You have a room. Great!

funFacts.title: Upstairs from the kahva
funFacts.body: Living above a café is a practical city pattern in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The commute is short, the coffee smell is strong, and neighbors already know your order. Ana’s soba above Amira’s puts her inside that everyday arrangement. Home vocabulary in this lesson starts in a real upstairs room, not a textbook floor plan.

funFacts.title: Stećci near Stolac
funFacts.body: Radimlja near Stolac is one of Herzegovina’s clearest outdoor history classrooms. Medieval stećci tombstones stand in open light among stone-house country. Emir uses the place as a postcard that widens Ana’s idea of home beyond one rented room. When you learn soba and kuća today, Stolac reminds you that home also has deep local roots.

funFacts.title: Stan vs kuća
funFacts.body: Bosnian separates apartment living from house living with clear everyday words. Stan means apartment, and kuća means house. Ana has a soba, a room, inside Amira’s world either way. Keep the three terms straight so you can describe where someone actually lives.

funFacts.title: Cat property law
funFacts.body: Mrvica follows a simple property rule. If she sits on a pillow, the pillow has a new owner. Ana can claim the room with imam, but the cat still claims the soft furniture. In this lesson, home vocabulary includes negotiating space with one very confident mačka.

civicContext.title: Return and property claims are still unfinished
civicContext.body: Housing return after the war remains an unfinished national task in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Hundreds of thousands of people were displaced from their homes. Annex 7 of the Dayton Peace Agreement promised the right to return and reclaim property, but many restitution cases, damaged apartments, and contested ownership claims stayed unresolved for years. Even now, some families are still waiting for permanent housing solutions that the peace settlement said should arrive much sooner.
